item.title: Sun Pharma Q2 net profit falls 36% on one-time charges, revenue rises 12%
item.description: Exceptional charges of Rs 1,268.8 crore, including a US antitrust settlement and Organon acquisition costs, weighed on profit, while India formulation sales grew 17.3 per cent ...
item.dc:creator: Anjali Singh
item.content:encoded: India’s largest drugmaker, Sun Pharmaceutical Industries, on Friday reported a 36 per cent year-on-year decline in consolidated net profit to Rs 1,988.5 crore for the second quarter of FY27, weighed down by exceptional charges. Revenue from operations rose 11.9 per cent to Rs 16,198.7 crore. The company reported exceptional charges of Rs 1,268.8 crore, comprising Rs 922.7 crore towards a settlement in a US antitrust litigation case and Rs 346.2 crore in expenses related to its proposed acquisition of Organon. Excluding exceptional items, adjusted net profit stood at Rs 3,162 crore, up 1.4 per cent year-on-year. EBITDA rose 4.8 per cent to Rs 4,743.9 crore, with margins at 29.3 per cent. The company said the margin was lower than a year earlier because the year-ago quarter had benefited from sales of generic lenalidomide, a product now facing erosion in the US. Gross margin improved to 80.8 per cent. The effective tax rate rose to 28.3 per cent from 24.7 per cent. The results were announced during market hours. Sun Pharma shares rose 0.8 per cent to close at Rs 1,778.25 on the BSE. “Our performance during the quarter was driven by strong momentum in India, Emerging Markets and Rest of World,” said Kirti Ganorkar, Managing Director. He highlighted the US approval of Ilumya for treating adults with active psoriatic arthritis and the preferred recommendation from the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) for Unloxcyt in advanced cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. India leads growth Formulation sales in India rose 17.3 per cent to Rs 5,552.3 crore, accounting for 34.5 per cent of consolidated sales. Sun Pharma’s market share increased to 8.6 per cent from 8.3 per cent, according to Pharmarack’s moving annual total (MAT) data for September 2026, retaining its position as the country’s largest pharmaceutical company. It ranked first by prescriptions in 12 doctor categories, according to SMSRC data. The company launched 14 new products during the quarter and 19 in the first half of FY27. US sales decline US formulation sales fell 8.2 per cent to $455 million, accounting for about 27 per cent of total sales, hurt by erosion in generic lenalidomide sales. However, sales grew 6.5 per cent sequentially, supported by five generic launches. On the earnings call, management also acknowledged a slowdown in Ilumya sales in the US. Richard Ashcroft, CEO of North America, said the causes were mixed. “I think there’s a bit of market, but frankly, part of it is execution as well, and that’s the intervention we’ve put in place,” he said. The global innovative medicines business grew 6.9 per cent to $356 million. Emerging markets formulation sales rose 7.6 per cent to $350 million, while rest-of-the-world formulation sales increased 3.1 per cent to $241 million. External active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) sales grew 13.7 per cent to Rs 488.9 crore. Organon acquisition on track On the proposed Organon acquisition, Sun Pharma said integration planning was progressing as scheduled, with regulatory approvals secured in most regions. The transaction remains on track for closure in the fourth quarter of FY27. The company indicated that acquisition-related expenses would continue to be recognised as it moves towards closing the transaction. R&D spending and guidance Research and development (R&D) expenditure for the quarter stood at Rs 778.4 crore, or 4.8 per cent of sales, with innovative R&D accounting for 32.4 per cent of the total. “These numbers are tracking lower than our intended R&D spend, but we expect the second half of the year to catch up with some of this R&D spend,” said Dilip Shanghvi, Chairman. Asked whether double-digit revenue growth in the first half would prompt an upgrade to its full-year guidance, management held firm. “We’ll stick to what guidance we have given at the beginning of the year,” the company said, referring to its high-single-digit revenue growth forecast.

item.title: Sebi eases FPI compliance, extends KYC review period from December 1
item.description: Sebi has extended KYC review intervals for certain foreign portfolio investors to two or eight years and removed a separate disclosure requirement, effective December 1 ...
item.dc:creator: Khushboo Tiwari
item.content:encoded: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) on Friday rationalised the periodicity of know-your-customer (KYC) reviews for foreign portfolio investors (FPIs), as part of measures to reduce repetitive compliance requirements. According to the regulator, the revised framework increases the periodicity from one year to two years, and from three years to eight years, for specified categories of FPIs. The revised framework will come into effect from December 1. The regulator also announced that it would be doing away with the separate requirement for FPIs, other than those investing only in government securities, to intimate changes in previously submitted information or provide a no-change declaration at the time of continuation of registration. Under the revised norms, the frequency of KYC review will depend on the jurisdiction, category and regulated status of the FPI. For FPIs in non-high-risk jurisdictions, the review period will be eight years for Category-I investors. For Category-II investors, regulated entities will be subject to review every eight years, while others will have to undergo it every two years. For Category-I FPIs in high-risk jurisdictions, the review will be required every eight years for those registered under Regulation 5(a)(i) (government and government-related investors), and every two years for others. For Category-II FPIs in high-risk jurisdictions, the review will be every two years. The periodicity applicable to FPIs investing only in government securities (GS-FPIs) and single window automatic and generalised access for trusted foreign investors (SWAGAT-FI) FPIs will remain unchanged.  For SWAGAT-FI FPIs, the KYC review period will continue to be 10 years. For GS-FPIs, the review will continue to follow the periodicity applicable to their respective bank accounts, as prescribed by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI). Sebi has also modified the provisions on continuation of registration. FPIs wishing to continue their registration for the subsequent block of three years will have to pay the fees to their designated depository participant (DDP). For SWAGAT-FI FPIs, the block is 10 years. The fees must be paid at least 15 days before the existing validity expires, to facilitate a smooth continuation process. Depositories, custodians and DDPs have been asked to make the necessary changes in their systems and processes and bring them to the notice of the FPIs concerned. The regulator said the measure seeks to rationalise requirements of a similar nature, reduce repetitive compliance and ease the compliance burden on FPIs. The move is part of its broader effort to reduce procedural requirements and provide a seamless, transparent and investor-friendly environment for FPIs, it said.

item.title: Sideloading on Android: What Google's new rules mean for rival app stores
item.description: Google's new Registered App Stores programme promises easier app installs and background updates for rival marketplaces on Android. But will it improve competition with Google Play?
item.dc:creator: Harsh Shivam
item.content:encoded: Google has opened enrollment for its Registered App Stores programme, which will allow approved third-party app marketplaces to install applications with a single tap and deliver updates in the background on supported Android devices from December 1. The programme gives alternative app stores a more direct route to reach Android users, but access to these features will depend on meeting Google's verification, security and operational requirements. The move does not introduce third-party app stores to Android. Users have been able to download alternative marketplaces such as Epic Games Store and F-Droid, or install applications directly through APK files, outside Google Play. However, these installations typically involve additional system prompts, manual permissions and separate confirmation for app updates.ALSO READ: WhatsApp adds group status, permanent pins, unread message filters and moreGoogle's new programme changes this installation process for marketplaces that qualify. Registered stores will be able to install apps without secondary system confirmation screens, while updates can be downloaded and installed in the background, subject to user settings. Users will also receive notifications about download progress and installation status. The programme is optional. Marketplaces that do not register can continue distributing applications through Android, although their installation experience will remain unchanged.What changes under Google's Registered App Stores programme?Under Android's existing sideloading process, users installing an alternative app store must allow it to install unknown applications through system settings. Each subsequent app installation also requires a separate confirmation. Updates distributed through these stores require user approval. Registered App Stores will receive permission to install applications directly through the Android system once the marketplace has been verified. This removes the additional confirmation screens for individual installations. The programme also allows registered marketplaces to manage app updates in the background, with users retaining control over automatic updates. However, registration is not an automatic approval for unrestricted app distribution. Google requires marketplaces to operate as legitimate, open platforms that allow eligible developers to distribute applications under clear and non-discriminatory policies. They must provide users with information about applications, including developer details, version information, download size and relevant safety disclosures. Marketplaces must also allow users to uninstall applications through the same listing or management page used to install them, support app restoration and archiving, and provide a mechanism to update the marketplace itself. There are financial and technical requirements as well. Ars Technica reported that the fee is $10,000 a year, with additional review charges possible if a store's catalogue exceeds Google's malware threshold.ALSO READ: Alphabet loses over $500 billion in market value as AI hits Google searchApplicants must register as organisations through the Android Developer Console, complete developer verification and establish ownership of their marketplace's package name. They must also submit their store's APK for malware scanning and provide Google with their complete app catalogue and subsequent updates for security review. Google can remove a marketplace from the programme if it fails to meet these requirements. However, the company states that registered stores remain responsible for their catalogues and that Google will not moderate the content distributed through them. The programme will be available from December 1, 2026, on devices running Android 17 QPR2 or later in supported regions, including India. It is not currently available in the US. The rollout will therefore depend on both regional availability and whether device manufacturers deliver the required Android update. Android Developers Ars TechnicaWhy is Google formalising third-party app stores?The programme is part of Google's broader changes to Android's app distribution and billing policies following its legal dispute with Epic Games, the developer of Fortnite. Epic sued Google in 2020, arguing that the company used its control over Android and Google Play to restrict competition in app distribution and in-app payments. In 2023, a US jury found Google had maintained an illegal monopoly in the Android app distribution and billing markets. A subsequent court injunction required Google to make changes that would allow competing app stores to reach Android users and compete with Google Play. Google challenged the ruling, but the legal dispute continued through subsequent proceedings. In November 2025, the companies announced a proposed settlement, followed by a revised agreement in March 2026. The changes included alternative billing options, lower service fees and a programme for registered third-party app stores. Google's March announcement presented the registration framework as a way to make alternative app stores easier to install while retaining security checks. Epic welcomed the changes, saying they would allow competing marketplaces to operate on Android and give developers more distribution options. However, the US rollout has a separate legal complication. Google and Epic's revised settlement requires court approval. Google has indicated that the Registered App Stores programme will initially operate outside the US, with its US availability dependent on the legal process. Google has also introduced separate arrangements for third-party stores to access Google Play's app catalogue in the US. The distinction is important because the registration programme is not a court-mandated requirement for every third-party store. It is a voluntary framework through which marketplaces can obtain additional Android system capabilities.Does Google become a gatekeeper for alternative app distribution?The registration framework raises questions about how much control Google should have over competing marketplaces on an operating system that has traditionally allowed users to install software from outside its official app store. Google's security requirements have a clear purpose. Requiring developer verification, malware scanning and regular catalogue checks can make it harder for malicious applications to circulate through third-party stores. Users also benefit from having fewer installation prompts and a more consistent update process. However, the programme creates a distinction between marketplaces that receive Google's approval and those that continue to operate outside the framework. While the latter can still distribute applications, they do not get the same installation and update capabilities. The requirement to share an entire app catalogue and subsequent updates with Google also gives the company visibility into applications distributed through competing stores. Google says this information is needed for malware review, while marketplaces remain responsible for their own content. The annual fee and organisational verification requirements could also prove difficult for smaller independent marketplaces. There is a further question about how Google will assess applications and enforce its requirements. The programme allows Google to suspend a store's registered status if it fails to meet the prescribed standards. Although this does not prevent the marketplace from continuing to operate through conventional sideloading, losing registration would mean losing the simplified installation experience. This makes the registration process an important point of control over how easily rival marketplaces can reach users, even if Google does not have exclusive authority over app distribution on Android.How does Google's approach compare with Apple's alternative app stores?Apple's approach to alternative app distribution offers a useful comparison, although the circumstances behind the changes are different. Unlike Android, Apple's iOS ecosystem traditionally did not allow users to install third-party app marketplaces. Developers had to distribute applications through the App Store, subject to Apple's review and commercial terms. Regulatory intervention forced Apple to change this model in the European Union under the Digital Markets Act (DMA). Starting with iOS 17.4 in March 2024, Apple allowed authorised alternative app marketplaces to distribute applications in the region. Developers can also distribute applications through their websites under certain conditions. Apple retains a verification process for marketplace operators and requires applications distributed outside the App Store to undergo notarisation. This is a baseline security review intended to identify malware, security threats and certain forms of fraud. Marketplace operators must also obtain Apple's authorisation and meet ongoing requirements. Japan has followed a similar route under its Mobile Software Competition Act. With iOS 26.2, Apple introduced alternative app marketplaces and other distribution options in the country, alongside requirements for marketplace authorisation and app notarisation. These changes came in response to the new Japanese law, rather than a voluntary decision by Apple to open its ecosystem. Google's framework differs in one important respect: Android already permits third-party app distribution. Its new programme does not create that right or make registration compulsory. It offers approved marketplaces additional operating system privileges that reduce the friction involved in installing and updating applications. Apple, meanwhile, has introduced alternative distribution in markets where regulation required it to do so, while retaining control over marketplace authorisation and baseline security checks. Both companies therefore retain a role in determining which marketplaces qualify for additional system-level capabilities. The difference lies in the starting point. Apple is opening distribution options in response to regulatory requirements, while Google is formalising an approval system for capabilities on an operating system that already supports sideloading. For Android users, the immediate change will be fewer steps when installing applications from registered marketplaces. Whether this leads to more competition will depend on how many alternative stores enrol, how accessible Google's requirements are to smaller operators and whether developers choose to distribute their applications outside Google Play.

item.title: Jio Platforms' Q2 profit up 13.7% in first results since blockbuster debut
item.description: Jio Platforms reported a 13.7% rise in Q2FY27 net profit to ₹8,389 crore, marking its first quarterly results since the telecom and digital major's record $3.2 billion stock market debut.
item.content:encoded:
Home / Companies / Quarterly Results / Jio Platforms Q2 profit rises 13.7% to ₹8,387 crore, revenue up 11.4%

Jio Platforms Q2 profit rises 13.7% to ₹8,387 crore, revenue up 11.4% JPL IPO broke records across all investor categories; a milestone for the next growth phase: MD Akash Ambani

The company listed on the BSE on October 28, raising Rs 30,188 crore in what was termed India's largest public offering

Gulveen Aulakh New Delhi 6 min read Last Updated : Oct 30 2026 | 8:41 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Jio Platforms Ltd (JPL), the parent company of India’s largest telecom services provider, Reliance Jio, reported a net profit of Rs 8,387 crore, up 13.7 per cent from Rs 7,379 crore in the same period the year before. Revenue rose 11.4 per cent to Rs 40,475 crore in Q2FY27 from Rs 36,332 crore in the same quarter last year. Sequentially, profit increased from Rs 7,764 crore in the previous quarter, while revenue rose from Rs 39,173 crore.   The company listed on the BSE on October 28, raising Rs 30,188 crore in what was termed India's largest public offering. "We were raising Rs 30,000 crore-odd, and we saw demand of over Rs 7.5 trillion. We saw every investor category broken, starting from QIB to small HNI, big HNI, retail, and all the various shareholders, employees, all of the categories were broken," Akash Ambani, managing director of Jio Platforms Ltd, said on the analyst call following the results.

The top executive at India's second-largest company by market capitalisation said that JPL's record-breaking IPO numbers reflected the Indian market at a time when it had seen outflows of more than Rs 48,000 crore led by foreign institutional investors (FIIs). "In a market situation like that, for us to make our debut, was very proud that the people were realizing of the business that we've spent, we've built... we put on our extreme hard work over the last 10 years to build this business, and we'll continue to do so," Ambani noted.   Ambani added that the IPO was a new milestone and that the company would move on from here. "We believe that you know the value that we can create over the next decade or so is even more than what we have done in our first decade, and we'll continue to aspire to that perspective," he said.   ALSO READ:  RIL Q2 profit jumps 40% on refining, digital gains; revenue hits record

Quarterly earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) climbed 16.6 per cent year-on-year to Rs 21,879 crore. The 250-basis-point rise in margins was driven by revenue growth and operating leverage. Jio reported average revenue per user (Arpu), a monthly metric of profitability for a telecom services provider, of Rs 218.8, marginally up from Rs 215.6 in Q1FY27. However, year-on-year, Arpu was up 3.5 per cent from Rs 211.4, with promotional schemes for fixed broadband customers offsetting the impact of a better subscriber mix and increased usage.   “We warmly welcome our new shareholders to the Jio Platforms family as we enter a new era as a listed company. This quarter’s results continue to reflect the strength of our 5G network, and the growing reach of our broadband and digital services,” Ambani said in a statement to the exchanges.   ALSO READ:  Reliance Retail Q2 profit falls 24.3%, revenue rises 5.8% to ₹80,220 cr

The company said in its statement to the stock exchanges that Rs 27,500 crore from the net proceeds of the IPO had been utilised towards prepayment, in full or in part, of the principal amount outstanding on certain external commercial borrowings availed of by Reliance Jio Infocomm Ltd, a material subsidiary of JPL, and the balance amount would be utilised towards general corporate purposes.   JPL's net debt declined 78.6 per cent to Rs 8,822 crore in Q2FY27 from Rs 41,161 crore in Q2FY26. Debt declined 7.5 per cent quarter-on-quarter from Rs 9,539 crore in Q1FY27. Finance costs rose 40.3 per cent to Rs 3,009 crore in Q2FY27 from Rs 2,145 crore in Q2FY26.

Reliance Jio ended September 2026 with 542.4 million users, including 300 million 5G subscribers, accounting for more than 56 per cent of its customer base. The carrier added 9.1 million subscribers during the quarter. Jio’s 5G data traffic in the fourth quarter reached 71.3 billion gigabytes, while total voice traffic rose 1.3 per cent to 1.52 trillion minutes. It added 66 million 5G customers over the last 12 months and 15 million over the past quarter. Customer engagement also remained robust, with data consumption at 44.2 GB per month, higher than 38.7 GB per month in the same period last year.

Total fixed broadband subscribers as of September 2026 stood at 30 million, with about 7.3 million additions over the last 12 months. Jio AirFiber had a total base of over 15.1 million subscribers, accounting for more than 75 per cent of fixed broadband additions during the last 12 months, the company said.   “Ahead of the curve investment on next generation technologies has been the foundation of Jio’s success over the past decade. We would continue to build our capabilities across satellite communications, 6G intellectual property and AI embedded in our core voice and data services as we create lasting value for all our stakeholders,” Ambani added.

He elaborated on the company's future strategy, noting that it was unlike a traditional telecom services provider, owing largely to its proprietary technology with an integrated 4G and 5G stack, unlicensed broadband radio (UBR), and now fixed wireless accounting for 50 per cent of its entire base. He added that Jio would double down on offerings to enterprises, as this would be a major growth opportunity, with India having 350,000 leased lines.   On expanding internationally, Ambani said that the company would be "very selective" about the markets it would enter. "We will not be selling our proprietary stacks as a hardware commission or our software as you know a SaaS service. What we imagine the business model here to be is to be a actually managed service partner with our customers. It's not going to be a heavy capex rollout. You won't see us going and putting up towers and fiber and infrastructure only. But this is something that we think that will be enabled because of the only proprietary stack that we have," he added.

Harping on the company's competitive advantage — owing to full-stack technology across seven layers, deep engineering and proprietary IP contribution — Ambani said Jio had multiple growth engines across mobility, home, enterprise and international markets. "We are the ones that have a clear path of growth and profitability improving with a very strong balance sheet, even before the IPO proceeds come to us," he added.   More From This Section
